Chapter Six: The Comedy of Manners—Social Rituals and Everyday Performance.
Have you ever noticed the little dance we all do in social situations? There’s this unspoken choreography—like the handshake when you first meet someone, or that polite nod to a neighbor on your way out. Even the forced laughter at a joke that just doesn’t quite land—all these tiny performances help keep the wheels of society turning.
But, if you look a bit deeper, there’s often a sense of awkwardness underneath. It’s like everyone’s just playing along, hoping nobody realizes they’re just acting out their part.
Picture this: you’re at a dinner party, juggling a plate of food and a glass of wine, trying to remember what you’re supposed to say. The conversation gently bounces from weather, to work, to the latest news—each carefully chosen to avoid stepping on anyone’s toes. Maybe there’s that moment you laugh a little too loudly at a story, then quickly glance around to see if anybody noticed. It’s a real dance of self-consciousness, a constant back-and-forth between honesty and politeness.
Most of us learn these rituals as kids. We’re taught to say “please” and “thank you,” take turns, and smile—even when we’re not really feeling it. Over time, these rules become automatic. But, let’s be honest, that underlying tension never totally disappears. There’s always that risk of saying the wrong thing, of breaking some unwritten rule.
Some customs are so baked-in, we barely notice them. Like bringing a gift to a party, sending thank-you notes, or asking “How are you?” even when we don’t expect—or want—a real answer. It can feel like everyone’s following the same script, a little afraid to go off-book.
And yet, there’s comfort in these routines. They give us structure—a sense we belong, and a map for navigating the messiness of human interaction. Even the most cynical among us can appreciate those small gestures—a door held open, a kind word, or a shared laugh over a little mishap. These moments smooth out the bumps in daily life.
But here’s the flip side: the comedy of manners also shows us where social connection falls short. Sometimes, these rituals feel empty, and trying to fit in gets downright exhausting. That’s when we start craving something real—conversations that go deeper, relationships that don’t feel like a performance.
Still, you can’t help but see the humor in it all. The endless small talk, those awkward silences, the elaborate etiquette at weddings and funerals—it’s all perfect material for a good laugh. And while poking fun at these rituals doesn’t make them disappear, it does make them easier to live with. It’s our way of recognizing the gap between how we act, and how we really feel.
